regiones/artico-norteamericano/resumen.texto: The coasts and tundra north of the treeline, from the Aleutians and Alaska to Labrador, including the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. Paleo-Eskimo hunters settled it around 2500 BC, and from the 12th and 13th centuries the Thule, ancestors of the Inuit, arrived from Alaska with dog sleds, kayaks and whaling. Russians, whalers, traders and missionaries arrived between the 18th and 20th centuries. Today the region includes Nunavut, created in 1999, and other territories with Inuit self-government.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/eras.0.re.texto: Hunters of the Paleoarctic tradition occupy northern and western Alaska. On the Aleutians, the Anangula site is about 9,000 years old. The Canadian Arctic remained uninhabited, in part under ice.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/eras.1.re.texto: The Arctic microblade tradition (Denbigh, Pre-Dorset, Independence) spread within a few centuries from Alaska to Greenland. From around 500 BC the Dorset culture occupied the eastern Arctic, while in the Bering Strait the Norton, Ipiutak and Old Bering Sea cultures developed, ancestors of the Yupik and the Inuit.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/eras.2.re.texto: From northern Alaska, the Thule expanded eastward between 1200 and 1300 and occupied the entire Canadian Arctic. The Dorset disappeared around 1300–1400. The first documented encounters with Europeans were those of Martin Frobisher on Baffin Island (1576–1578), who took captives to England.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/eras.3.re.texto: After Bering’s voyage (1741), Russian fur hunters subjugated the Aleut and forced them to hunt sea otters. Shelikhov conquered Kodiak in 1784 with the Awa’uq massacre. The Russian-American Company (1799) governed Alaska until its sale to the United States in 1867.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/eras.4.re.texto: American and Scottish whalers, Hudson’s Bay Company traders and missionaries reached almost every community. From the 1950s governments concentrated the Inuit in permanent settlements. In 1953 Canada relocated families from Inukjuak to the High Arctic.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/eras.5.re.texto: The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (1971), the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement (1975) and the Nunavut Agreement (1993) recognized land and self-governing bodies. Nunavut separated from the Northwest Territories in 1999.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/demografi.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

Known from Dorset art (ivory carvings, masks) and from burials.
It arrived with the monks of Valaam at Kodiak in 1794, and it remains the church of most Aleut and of many Alutiiq and Yupik people.

Only in Alaska and the Aleutians; the rest of the North American Arctic was uninhabited.
They are the direct ancestors of the Yupik and the Inuit.
The Aleutians have been inhabited for about 9,000 years (Anangula). The continuity between these first settlers and the historical Unangan is debated.

Thule expansion eastward is now dated between 1200 and 1300 (Friesen and Arnold, 2008), later than previously thought. According to ancient DNA (Raghavan et al., 2014), the Thule and the Dorset were distinct populations that barely mixed.
The Russians never numbered more than a few hundred. The “creoles,” children of Russians and Indigenous women, were more numerous.

regiones/artico-norteamericano/idiomas.8.texto: In Alaska, English has largely replaced Inupiaq, Alutiiq and Aleut. In Nunavut and Nunavik most Inuit still speak Inuktitut.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/resume.texto: The boreal forest of Alaska and Canada, south of the tundra and north of the prairies and the Great Lakes, including Newfoundland and the interior of Labrador. It was inhabited by mobile hunters, fishers and trappers, at very low population densities: Athabaskan or Dene peoples in the west and Algonquian peoples (Cree, Innu, Northern Ojibwe) in the east. From 1670 it was the fur-trade territory of the Hudson’s Bay Company. The numbered treaties (1871–1921), mining, oil and dams transformed the region in the 20th century.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/eras.0.texto: Hunters of the Nenana and Denali complexes camped in the Tanana valley, in Alaska (Swan Point, Broken Mammoth), about 14,000 years ago. Much of the east remained under ice for several more millennia and was settled later.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/eras.1.texto: Small bands hunted caribou and moose and fished in lakes, using bark canoes, snowshoes and sleds. Some authors link the White River eruption, which covered southern Yukon with ash around the year 850, to the migration of Athabaskan peoples to the south.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/eras.2.texto: Basque whalers hunted in the Strait of Belle Isle from the 1530s (Red Bay), and the French traded with the Innu at Tadoussac from 1600. The Beothuk of Newfoundland avoided contact with Europeans.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/eras.3.texto: The Hudson’s Bay Company (1670) and the Northwest Company (1779) organized the fur trade with the Cree, Ojibwe, Chipewyan and other peoples, and the Métis emerged. The smallpox epidemic of 1781–1782 killed much of the population of the interior. Shanawdithit, the last known Beothuk, died in 1829.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/eras.4.texto: Rupert’s Land passed to Canada (1870), and the numbered treaties (1871–1921) ceded almost all of the territory in exchange for reserves and annuities, on terms whose scope the signatory peoples still dispute. The Klondike gold rush (1896–1899) and residential schools changed the lives of the Dene and the Cree.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/eras.5.texto: Dams (James Bay, from 1971), oil (the Athabasca oil sands, the Alaska pipeline) and mining transformed the region. The Alaska (1971), James Bay (1975) and Yukon (1993) agreements recognized land and self-governing bodies.

regiones/subartico-norteamericano/demogr.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

Anglicans, Methodists and other Protestant churches

Algonquian peoples (Cree, Innu, Naskapi, Northern Ojibwe)

People of European origin (Newfoundlanders, English-speaking Canadians, Americans)
The Bluefish Caves, in Yukon, are said to contain cut bones about 24,000 years old (Bourgeon et al., 2017). The interpretation is disputed.
It is not known how long they have occupied their historical territory. The date is approximate.

By population, since the mid-19th century: Newfoundland, the Saguenay and, later, the mining and oil cities, Anchorage and Fairbanks. Across most of the territory, the Dene, Cree and Innu peoples remain the majority.

regiones/costa-noroeste/resumen.texto: The strip of coast, islands and fjords between Yakutat Bay, in Alaska, and southern Oregon, covered by temperate rainforest. Its peoples, salmon fishers without agriculture, lived in villages of plank houses with chiefs, nobles, commoners and slaves. They raised carved poles and redistributed wealth at potlatches. From 1774 Spanish, British, Russian and American traders arrived for sea otter pelts. Epidemics, colonization and the Canadian ban on the potlatch (1885–1951) struck these societies hard.

regiones/costa-noroeste/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Manis mastodon, in Washington, with a bone point embedded in it, is about 13,800 years old. On Haida Gwaii and in southeastern Alaska there are sites more than 10,000 years old, which support the hypothesis of a coastal route of settlement.

regiones/costa-noroeste/eras.1.resumen.texto: With salmon fishing and smoking, permanent villages grew, with cedar plank houses, social inequality and wars to take slaves. At Ozette, on Cape Flattery, a mudslide buried several Makah houses with all their contents around 1700.

regiones/costa-noroeste/eras.2.resumen.texto: Juan Pérez reached Haida Gwaii in 1774 and Cook reached Nootka in 1778. The Nootka Crisis (1789–1794) pitted Spain against Great Britain. The Russians founded Sitka (1799) and the British Fort Vancouver (1825), while smallpox and fevers reduced the population.

regiones/costa-noroeste/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Oregon Treaty (1846) divided the coast between the United States and Great Britain. The smallpox epidemic of 1862, which arrived from Victoria, killed a large part of the peoples of the British Columbia coast. Canada banned the potlatch in 1885 and confiscated ceremonial objects, and both countries created reserves and residential schools.

regiones/costa-noroeste/eras.4.resumen.texto: Canada lifted the potlatch ban in 1951, and canoes, poles and languages returned. The Nisga’a treaty (2000) was the first modern treaty in British Columbia. The coast is now home to Seattle, Portland, Vancouver and Victoria.

regiones/costa-noroeste/demografia.0.not.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

regiones/costa-noroeste/religiones.0.nom.texto: Northwest Coast religions (guardian spirits, winter dance societies, first-salmon ceremony, potlatch)

regiones/costa-noroeste/religiones.3.nom.texto: Indigenous Shaker Church and traditional ceremonies

regiones/costa-noroeste/religiones.4.not.texto: In the 2021 Canadian census, more than half of the population of British Columbia reported no religion.

regiones/costa-noroeste/culturas.2.nombr.texto: British, American and Spanish traders, missionaries and settlers

regiones/costa-noroeste/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Whether its origin predates or postdates contact is debated.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/resumen.texto: The plateaus and valleys between the Cascade Range and the Rockies, watered by the Columbia and Fraser rivers: the interior of British Columbia, eastern Washington and Oregon, northern Idaho and western Montana. Its peoples, who spoke Salishan and Sahaptian languages, lived by salmon fishing at falls and rapids such as Celilo and Kettle Falls, by gathering roots such as camas, and by hunting. They traded between the coast and the plains. The horse arrived around 1730. Then came Lewis and Clark (1805), missions, the treaties of 1855 and the wars that ended with the Nez Perce War (1877).

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.1.nomb.texto: Fishers and gatherers of the Plateau

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.0.resu.texto: The Cooper’s Ferry site, in Idaho, has tools about 16,000 years old, among the oldest in the Americas (Davis et al., 2019). The Kennewick Man, about 9,000 years old, was the subject of a long legal dispute between scientists and tribes, which ended with his burial in 2017.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.1.resu.texto: Villages of semi-subterranean houses along the rivers, salmon fishing with nets and harpoons, and root gathering. Celilo Falls, on the Columbia, was for millennia the largest market in the region.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.2.resu.texto: Horses arrived around 1730 from the south, through the Shoshone. The Nez Perce, Cayuse and others adopted Plains customs and crossed the Rockies to hunt bison. Smallpox arrived in the 1770s and 1780s, before the Europeans did.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.3.resu.texto: Lewis and Clark crossed the region in 1805, and fur companies set up posts. Protestant (Whitman, 1836) and Jesuit (De Smet, 1841) missions arrived, along with settlers on the Oregon Trail. In 1847, after a measles epidemic, a group of Cayuse killed the Whitmans and eleven other people.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.4.resu.texto: The treaties of 1855 created the Yakama, Umatilla and Nez Perce reserves. The Yakama War (1855–1858) and the Nez Perce War (1877) followed, when Chief Joseph tried to reach Canada. No treaties were signed in the interior of British Columbia.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/eras.5.resu.texto: The Dalles Dam flooded Celilo Falls in 1957, and the dams on the Columbia blocked the salmon run. The tribes recovered fishing rights in the courts, as in the Belloni decision (Sohappy v. Smith, 1969) on the Columbia.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/demografia..texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/religiones..texto: Plateau religions (quest for the guardian spirit, winter dance, first foods ceremonies)
Washat or Dreamer religion (Smohalla) and the Indigenous Shaker Church

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/culturas.2..texto: Plateau peoples (Nez Perce, Yakama, Umatilla, Cayuse, Wasco, Interior Salish, Kutenai, Klamath and others)

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/culturas.4..texto: Americans and Canadians of European origin

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/culturas.0..texto: The date for Cooper’s Ferry is more widely accepted than those of other pre-Clovis sites, but it is not unanimous.

regiones/meseta-del-columbia/culturas.2..texto: The starting date is conventional: it marks the spread of semi-subterranean village houses.

regiones/gran-cuenca/resumen.texto: The region of endorheic basins between the Sierra Nevada and the Rockies, including Nevada, Utah, southern Idaho, southeastern Oregon, and western Colorado and Wyoming. Its peoples—Paiute, Shoshone, Ute and Washoe—lived in small bands that moved with the seasons between lakes, mountains and deserts, gathering pine nuts and seeds and organizing communal rabbit and pronghorn hunts. From 1847 Mormons colonized Utah, and silver in Nevada (1859) drew miners. The two Ghost Dances (1870 and 1889) came out of this region.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.0.resumen.texto: Human coprolites from Paisley Caves, in Oregon, are about 14,300 years old, and the mummy from Spirit Cave, in Nevada, is about 10,600. They belong to the Western Stemmed Point tradition, contemporary with Clovis.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Danger, Hogup and Lovelock caves preserved baskets, sandals and decoys of woven rush: a life centered on lakes and marshes that were drying up.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.2.resumen.texto: In Utah, the Fremont grew maize, lived in pit-house villages, and left rock art and clay figurines until their disappearance around 1300. In the rest of the region, hunter-gatherers continued.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.3.resumen.texto: Paiute, Shoshone and Ute peoples occupied the whole region, perhaps after an expansion from the southwestern Great Basin. Utes and Shoshones adopted the horse in the 17th and 18th centuries; the southern Paiute continued on foot.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.4.resumen.texto: The Domínguez and Escalante expedition (1776) traveled through Utah. Along the Old Spanish Trail (1829–1848), Utes and New Mexicans took Paiute captives, mostly children, to sell as servants in New Mexico and California.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Mormons arrived in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, and the Comstock silver (1859) populated Nevada. In the Bear River Massacre (1863), California volunteers killed about 250 Shoshone or more. The Paiute prophets Wodziwob (1870) and Wovoka (1889) began the Ghost Dances.

regiones/gran-cuenca/eras.6.resumen.texto: The reservations are small and scattered. Salt Lake City and Las Vegas grew in the 20th century with irrigation, mining, military bases and, in Las Vegas, gambling.

regiones/gran-cuenca/demografia.0.nota.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

regiones/gran-cuenca/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Great Basin religions (shamans, circle dance, dreams and visions)

regiones/gran-cuenca/religiones.2.nombre.texto: Mormonism (The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints)

regiones/gran-cuenca/religiones.3.nombre.texto: Ghost Dance, Native American Church and traditional ceremonies

regiones/gran-cuenca/religiones.4.nombre.texto: Christianity (Mormons, Catholics and Protestants, with no majority among them)

regiones/gran-cuenca/culturas.3.nombre.texto: Numic peoples (Paiute, Shoshone, Ute) and Washoe

regiones/gran-cuenca/culturas.5.nombre.texto: Americans of European origin (in Utah, mostly Mormons)

regiones/gran-cuenca/culturas.3.nota.texto: Lamb (1958) proposed that the Numic languages spread from the southwestern Great Basin around the year 1000. It is the most cited hypothesis, but its date and its form are debated.

regiones/gran-cuenca/idiomas.1.nombre.texto: Numic languages (Paiute, Shoshone, Ute) and Washoe

regiones/gran-cuenca/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Washoe is not Uto-Aztecan: it is a language isolate.

regiones/california-indigena/resumen.texto: California west of the Sierra Nevada and the desert, from the Oregon border to the Mexican border, with the Channel Islands. Without agriculture, its peoples reached some of the highest population densities in North America thanks to acorns, fish and shellfish, and spoke more than eighty languages. The Franciscan missions (1769–1834), the gold rush and the massacres that followed reduced the Indigenous population to a fraction of its original size.

regiones/california-indigena/eras.4.nomb.texto: Mexico, the gold rush and the massacres

regiones/california-indigena/eras.0.resu.texto: The remains of the Arlington Springs man, on Santa Rosa Island, are about 13,000 years old: those who lived there must have arrived by sea. Shell middens of the same age are found on the Channel Islands.

regiones/california-indigena/eras.1.resu.texto: Seed gatherers who ground them in mortars and metates and, on the coast, fishers and shellfish collectors.

regiones/california-indigena/eras.2.resu.texto: Acorns, ground and leached to remove the tannin, sustain large, stable villages. The Chumash build plank canoes (tomol) and use shell beads as money; in the northwest, the Yurok, Karuk and Hupa hold world renewal ceremonies.

regiones/california-indigena/eras.3.resu.texto: From San Diego (1769), the Franciscans founded twenty-one missions along the coast; baptized Indigenous people were bound to the mission, escape was punished, and mortality from disease was very high. Mexico secularized the missions in 1834.

regiones/california-indigena/eras.4.resu.texto: After secularization, many Indigenous people remained as laborers on the ranchos. With the American conquest (1846–1848) and the gold rush, militias, volunteers and the army killed thousands of Indigenous people—between 9,500 and 16,000 according to Madley (2016), who calls it genocide—and an 1850 law allowed them to be subjected to servitude.

regiones/california-indigena/eras.5.resu.texto: After the Modoc War (1872–1873), the survivors remained in small rancherías and reservations, and many tribes were not recognized by the federal government until the 20th century. California became the most populous state in the United States.

regiones/california-indigena/demografia..texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker's total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people; other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million. For California, Kroeber (1925) calculated about 133,000 inhabitants and Cook (1976) about 310,000, both at the time of contact.

regiones/california-indigena/religiones..texto: Religions of California (Kuksu in the center, the toloache cult in the south, world renewal in the northwest)
Around 1820, about 21,000 Indigenous people lived in the missions.

regiones/california-indigena/culturas.2..texto: Peoples of California (Chumash, Tongva, Ohlone, Miwok, Pomo, Maidu, Yokuts, Wintun, Yurok, Hupa and many others)

regiones/california-indigena/culturas.3..texto: Spanish and Mexican soldiers, missionaries and settlers (Californios)

regiones/california-indigena/culturas.4..texto: Americans (of European, Latin American, Asian and African origin)

regiones/california-indigena/culturas.2..texto: According to Cook (1976), the Indigenous population fell from about 150,000 in 1848 to about 30,000 in 1870.

regiones/california-indigena/culturas.4..texto: Since around 2014, Hispanics have been the largest group in California.

regiones/california-indigena/idiomas.1.n.texto: More than eighty languages from about twenty families (Uto-Aztecan, Athabaskan, Algic, Yokuts, Miwok-Costanoan, Pomo and others)

regiones/california-indigena/idiomas.6.n.texto: Indigenous languages, almost all extinct or endangered

regiones/california-indigena/idiomas.1.n.texto: California was one of the most linguistically diverse regions of the world; the Hokan and Penutian groupings, which bring together several of these families, are debated hypotheses.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/resumen.texto: Arizona, New Mexico, western Texas, and southern Colorado and Utah: deserts, plateaus and mountains where maize arrived from Mexico by around 2100 BC. The Hohokam flourished there with their irrigation canals, as did the ancestral Puebloans of Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde, whose descendants—the Hopi, the Zuni and the Rio Grande Pueblos—still live on their lands; Apaches and Navajos arrived from the north around the 15th and 16th centuries. It was a frontier of New Spain from 1598, the scene of the Pueblo Revolt (1680), and passed to the United States in 1848.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.4..texto: Rio Grande Pueblos and the arrival of Apaches and Navajos

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.7..texto: New Mexico and the Pimería Alta

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.0..texto: The human footprints at White Sands, in New Mexico, have been dated to 23,000–21,000 years ago, a date that is still debated. Then come the Clovis and Folsom hunters, who hunted mammoths and ancient bison.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.1..texto: Hunter-gatherers of the desert tradition (Cochise), with grinding stones and basketry.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.2..texto: Maize arrives from Mexico around 2100 BC; at Las Capas, next to Tucson, there are irrigation canals from around 1200 BC. Pithouse villages and pottery appear.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.3..texto: The Hohokam irrigate the Phoenix valley with hundreds of kilometers of canals; at Chaco Canyon (850–1150) large houses linked by roads are built, and at Mesa Verde, cliff dwellings. The great drought of 1276–1299 and violence led to the abandonment of the Four Corners region around 1300.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.4..texto: The ancestral Puebloans concentrate in large villages along the Rio Grande, at Zuni and at Hopi, where the cult of the kachinas spreads. The Hohokam disappear around 1450 and are succeeded by the O'odham; the Southern Athabaskans, ancestors of the Apaches and Navajos, arrive from the north.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.5..texto: Coronado's expedition (1540–1542) takes Zuni and attacks the Tiguex pueblos. Oñate founds New Mexico in 1598 and, after the resistance of Acoma (1599), sentences the men over 25 to lose a foot and to twenty years of servitude; it is not known how many had the amputation carried out.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.6..texto: In August 1680 the Pueblos, coordinated by Popé, killed some 400 settlers, including 21 Franciscans, and drove the Spanish as far as El Paso. Diego de Vargas retook Santa Fe in 1692.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.7..texto: Spanish and Pueblo peoples ally against attacks by Comanches, Apaches and Navajos; in the Pimería Alta, Eusebio Kino founds missions among the O'odham from 1687. After Mexican independence, the region passed to the United States with the war of 1846–1848.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.8..texto: The United States Army forces the Navajos on the “Long Walk” to Bosque Redondo (1864–1868), where many died of hunger and disease, and fights the Apaches until Geronimo's surrender in 1886.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/eras.9..texto: The Navajo reservation is the largest in the United States. Arizona and New Mexico have been states since 1912, and since the mid-20th century Phoenix, Tucson, Albuquerque and El Paso have grown thanks to irrigation, military bases and migration.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/demogra.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker's total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people; other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million. This is the highest figure of the ten areas: it probably includes peoples of northern Mexico (Yaquis, Mayos, Tarahumaras and others) that the Handbook treats within the Southwest and that on this map are in Aridoamerica.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/religio.texto: Religions of the Southwest (kivas and, from the 14th century, the kachina cult among the Pueblos; Navajo and Apache ceremonies)
Christianity (Hispanic and Indigenous Catholics, Anglo-American Protestants)
Native American Church among the Navajos
The Franciscans persecuted Pueblo ceremonies and destroyed masks and kivas, one of the causes of the 1680 revolt.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/cultura.texto: Farmers of Oasisamerica: Hohokam, Mogollon and Ancestral Puebloans; later, Pueblos, O'odham and Yuman peoples
Pueblos (Hopi, Zuni and Rio Grande Pueblos)
New Mexicans (Spanish, criollos, mestizos and genízaros)
New Mexicans (Spanish, criollos, mestizos and genízaros)
Hispanics of New Mexico and southern Arizona

The White Sands remains have been dated to 23,000–21,000 years using seeds and pollen (Bennett et al., 2021; Pigati et al., 2023); other researchers object to these dates. Secure occupation begins with Clovis, around 11000 BC.
Their arrival is dated between 1300 and 1525 depending on the authors; most place it around 1400–1500.
In the 17th century the settlers of New Mexico numbered a few thousand, against tens of thousands of Pueblo Indians.
They remained the majority of New Mexico's population until the early 20th century.

regiones/suroeste-norteamericano/idiomas.texto: Uto-Aztecan (O'odham, Hopi), Tanoan (Tewa, Tiwa, Towa), Keresan, Zuni and Yuman languages
Some linguists (Hill, 2001) propose that speakers of Uto-Aztecan languages brought maize from Mexico; the hypothesis is debated.
Navajo is the Indigenous language with the most speakers in the United States, but in the region it is a minority next to English and Spanish.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/resumen.texto: The prairies and steppes between the Mississippi and the Rockies, from Alberta and Manitoba to central Texas. For millennia they were the land of bison hunters and, along the Missouri and its tributaries, of farming villages; with the horse, which arrived from New Mexico after 1680, the horse cultures of the Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche or Blackfoot emerged. American and Canadian colonization in the 19th century, the near extinction of the bison and the wars of 1854–1890 ended them and led the peoples to reservations.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.0.resumen.texto: At Buttermilk Creek, in Texas, there are tools about 15,500 years old, a disputed date; Blackwater Draw, next to Clovis, and Folsom, in New Mexico, gave their names to the first cultures of mammoth and ancient bison hunters.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.1.resumen.texto: Bison hunters who used jumps, such as Head-Smashed-In, in Alberta, used for more than 5,000 years.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.2.resumen.texto: Pottery, burial mounds and the first crops in the east; in the west, bison hunters continue.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.3.resumen.texto: Fortified farming villages along the Missouri, ancestors of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara. At Crow Creek, in South Dakota, a pit from around 1325 holds the remains of some 480 people killed in an attack; Coronado reached Quivira, among the Wichita, in 1541.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.4.resumen.texto: Horses, spread from New Mexico after the 1680 revolt, and then firearms allow the Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche, Kiowa and Blackfoot to live by hunting bison on horseback. The smallpox epidemic of 1837 nearly destroyed the Mandan, and American expansion brought wars, with massacres such as Sand Creek (1864) and battles such as Little Bighorn (1876).

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.5.resumen.texto: The United States seizes the Black Hills (1877) and divides the reservations into allotments (Dawes Act, 1887); at Wounded Knee (1890) the army killed some 250 Lakota or more. In Canada, Treaties 1 to 7 (1871–1877) and the defeat of the North-West Rebellion (1885) opened the prairies to settlement.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/eras.6.resumen.texto: The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) restored some self-government to the tribes, and in 1973 the American Indian Movement occupied Wounded Knee for 71 days. The Plains are one of the great agricultural regions of the world.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/demografia.0.n.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/religiones.0.n.texto: Plains religions (vision quest, sacred pipe, Sun Dance, medicine societies)

regiones/grandes-llanuras/religiones.1.n.texto: Catholicism of the missions of Texas and St. Louis

regiones/grandes-llanuras/religiones.4.n.texto: Plains religions and the Ghost Dance (1889–1890)

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.1.nom.texto: Bison hunters and, in the east, Plains Woodland farmers

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.2.nom.texto: Missouri farming villages and bison hunters on foot

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.3.nom.texto: Plains horse peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche, Kiowa, Blackfoot, Crow, Pawnee, Osage and others)

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.4.nom.texto: Spaniards and Tejanos of San Antonio

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.5.nom.texto: French and Creoles of St. Louis and Métis traders

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.6.nom.texto: Americans and Canadians of European origin

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.0.not.texto: The tools from the Debra L. Friedkin site, at Buttermilk Creek, have been dated to about 15,500 years (Waters et al., 2011); the date is debated.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/culturas.6.not.texto: Settlers outnumbered Indigenous peoples from the 1830s and 1840s in Missouri, Iowa and Texas, and from the 1880s in the western plains.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/idiomas.1.nomb.texto: Plains languages: Siouan, Caddoan (Pawnee, Arikara, Wichita), Algonquian (Cheyenne, Arapaho, Blackfoot, Cree), Athabaskan (Apache), Kiowa and Comanche

regiones/grandes-llanuras/idiomas.2.nomb.texto: Siouan languages (Lakota, Dakota, Crow, Mandan, Hidatsa, Omaha, Osage)

regiones/grandes-llanuras/idiomas.5.nomb.texto: Siouan languages and other Indigenous languages

regiones/grandes-llanuras/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No single family included most of the peoples; Plains Sign Language served among peoples who spoke different languages.

regiones/grandes-llanuras/idiomas.2.nota.texto: It is the family with the most peoples on the Plains; some, such as the Lakota, arrived from the east in the 17th and 18th centuries.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/resumen.texto: The forests of the Atlantic coast, the St. Lawrence valley, the Great Lakes and the Ohio valley, from Nova Scotia and Quebec to Virginia and Illinois. It was the land of Algonquian and Iroquoian peoples who combined the cultivation of maize, beans and squash with hunting and fishing, heirs of the Adena and Hopewell cultures; at its western edge was the Mississippian city of Cahokia. From the 17th century, French, Dutch and English settlers founded colonies there, and the region became the center of American independence and of the formation of Canada.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.0.resu.texto: The Meadowcroft Rockshelter, in Pennsylvania, would contain occupations about 16,000 years old, a disputed date; the Debert site, in Nova Scotia, and Bull Brook, in Massachusetts, show caribou hunters from the late Pleistocene.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.1.resu.texto: Hunters, fishers and gatherers; in the Great Lakes, the Old Copper Complex has worked native copper for more than 8,000 years.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.2.resu.texto: Pottery and the first crops appear; in the Ohio valley, the Adena (first millennium BC) and Hopewell (around 100 BC–AD 500) cultures built mounds and earthworks and traded obsidian, copper and shells from across the continent.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.3.resu.texto: Maize becomes the main crop; the Iroquois live in villages of longhouses with palisades and form the Confederacy of the Five Nations, whose founding is dated between 1142 and the early 17th century depending on the authors. At the western edge, Cahokia (1050–1350) was the largest city north of Mexico.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.4.resu.texto: Jamestown (1607), Quebec (1608), Plymouth (1620) and New Amsterdam (1625) are founded; the epidemics of 1616–1619 and 1633 emptied the New England coast. The Beaver Wars scattered the Huron (1649), and the Pequot War (1636–1638), King Philip's War (1675–1676) and the French and Indian War (1754–1763) decided British dominance.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.5.resu.texto: The Proclamation of 1763 limited settlement to the west of the Appalachians; after American independence (1776–1783), Loyalists moved to Canada. The Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) and the death of Tecumseh (1813) opened the Ohio valley to settlers.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/eras.6.resu.texto: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 expelled most peoples south of the Great Lakes to the west. The region industrialized and received millions of immigrants; Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick formed the Canadian Confederation in 1867.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/demografia..texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/religiones..texto: Eastern woodlands religions (manitou and orenda, shamans, the Ojibwe Midewiwin society, the Huron Feast of the Dead)
Catholicism (missions in Huronia from 1615, New France and Maryland)
Catholicism (New France and Quebec, Maryland and later Irish and Italian immigration)
Protestantism (Anglicans, Congregationalists, Quakers, Presbyterians, Lutherans, Baptists, Methodists)
Christianity (Catholics and Protestants in similar proportions)

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/culturas.3..texto: Algonquian peoples (Lenape, Wampanoag, Powhatan, Mi'kmaq, Ojibwe, Shawnee, Miami, Illinois and others)

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/culturas.4..texto: Iroquoian peoples (Haudenosaunee, Huron, Neutral, Erie, Susquehannock)

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/culturas.5..texto: Cahokia and other Mississippian peoples of the middle Mississippi valley

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/culturas.11.texto: English, Scots-Irish and German settlers of the Thirteen Colonies

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/culturas.0..texto: The date for Meadowcroft (about 16,000 years) has been debated since the 1970s.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/culturas.8..texto: New France had about 15,000 people of European origin around 1700.

regiones/bosques-del-noreste/idiomas.1.n.texto: Roger Williams published a Narragansett vocabulary (1643), and the Bible that John Eliot translated into Massachusett with Indigenous collaborators (1663) was the first complete Bible printed in America.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/resumen.texto: The coastal plains, valleys and hills of the southern United States, from North Carolina and Tennessee to Florida, Louisiana, and eastern Texas and Oklahoma. Here the oldest mounds in North America were built (Watson Brake, Poverty Point), and the Mississippian chiefdoms of Moundville, Etowah and Spiro flourished; after the Spanish expeditions and the epidemics, their survivors formed the Creek, Cherokee, Choctaw and Chickasaw nations. The plantation economy with enslaved Africans and the Indian Removal Act of 1830, with the Trail of Tears, completely changed their population.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.4.n.texto: Spanish expeditions, epidemics and the Indian slave trade

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.0.r.texto: At Page-Ladson, on a Florida river, there are stone tools and mastodon bones about 14,550 years old (Halligan et al., 2016).

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.1.r.texto: Watson Brake, in Louisiana, has mounds from around 3500 BC, the oldest in North America, and Poverty Point (around 1700–1100 BC) was a great center of earthworks. At Stallings Island, in Georgia, one of the oldest pottery traditions in North America was made.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.2.r.texto: Pottery, villages and mounds; Marksville and Swift Creek take part in the Hopewell network, and Weeden Island flourishes in Florida and Georgia.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.3.r.texto: Chiefdoms with plazas and earthen platforms that supported temples and the houses of chiefs: Moundville, Etowah, Spiro, Coosa, Apalachee. Many centers were depopulated or reorganized before the arrival of Europeans.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.4.r.texto: Ponce de León arrives in Florida in 1513; Hernando de Soto's expedition (1539–1543) crosses the region and at Mabila (1540) kills thousands of Tascalusa's warriors, according to its chroniclers. Spain founds St. Augustine (1565) and missions among the Timucua and Apalachee; from Carolina (1670), English traders buy and sell tens of thousands of enslaved Indigenous people until the Yamasee War (1715).

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.5.r.texto: Creeks, Cherokees, Choctaws and Chickasaws trade and negotiate with the British, the French (New Orleans, 1718) and the Spanish; the Natchez are destroyed by the French in 1729–1731. Plantations of rice, indigo and then cotton expand with enslaved African labor.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.6.r.texto: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 deports the five nations to Indian Territory; on the Cherokee Trail of Tears (1838–1839) about 4,000 people died, according to the most cited estimate. The Civil War (1861–1865) ends slavery.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/eras.7.r.texto: Reconstruction, racial segregation and the struggle for civil rights, which culminates in the laws of 1964 and 1965. The region still has the Eastern Cherokee, the Seminole and Miccosukee of Florida, and the Choctaw of Mississippi.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/demograf.texto: Estimate for around 1500, summed town by town from the volumes of the Handbook of North American Indians (Smithsonian). Ubelaker’s total for the United States and Canada is 1,894,350 people. Other authors propose much higher figures, such as Dobyns (1983), with about 18 million.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/religion.texto: Southeastern religions (sacred fire, Green Corn Ceremony)
Protestantism (Baptists and Methodists, the majority since the 19th century)
Its symbols—the hawk man, the cross in the circle, the eye in the hand—are documented mainly between 1200 and 1650.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/culturas.texto: Southeastern peoples (Creeks, Cherokees, Choctaws, Chickasaws, Natchez, Caddos, Timucuas, Apalachee)
Eastern Cherokees, Seminoles, Mississippi Choctaws and others
Hispanics (Cubans in Florida since 1959, Mexicans and Central Americans)
In 1860 they were about 40% of the population of the South and more than half in South Carolina and Mississippi.

regiones/sudeste-norteamericano/idiomas..texto: Muskogean languages (Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Apalachee, Alabama)
Timucua, Calusa and other Florida languages

Many Mississippian chiefdoms are assumed to have spoken Muskogean languages, but there is no direct evidence. Alongside them were languages of other families or isolates: Cherokee (Iroquoian), Caddo, Natchez, Timucua, Yuchi.

Timucua, an isolate, is the first Indigenous language of the present-day United States with printed books: the bilingual catechisms and confessionals of Friar Francisco Pareja (1612–1627). Its last speakers left for Cuba with the Spanish in 1763.

regiones/area-maya/resumen.texto: Southeastern Mexico (Yucatán, Campeche, Quintana Roo, Tabasco and Chiapas), Guatemala, Belize, and western Honduras and El Salvador: the land of the Maya, from the jungles of Petén to the volcanic highlands. There developed city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán, with a logosyllabic writing system capable of recording their language, calendars that combined a 260-day ritual cycle, the 365-day year and the Long Count, and frequent wars between dynasties. After the Spanish conquest (1524–1697) the Maya remained the majority of the population until the 20th century, and today they are an important part of it, especially in Guatemala and Yucatán.

regiones/area-maya/eras.0.resumen.texto: In the submerged cave of Hoyo Negro, in Quintana Roo, the skeleton of a teenager, Naia, about 12,000–13,000 years old, was found. Maize cultivation spread through the lowlands between 3000 and 2000 BC.

regiones/area-maya/eras.1.resumen.texto: Farming villages and then large centers: Aguada Fénix (around 1000 BC), Nakbé and El Mirador in Petén, Kaminaljuyu in the highlands. The murals of San Bartolo (around 100 BC) already show writing and sacred kingship.

regiones/area-maya/eras.2.resumen.texto: Dozens of kingdoms with dynasties that recorded their dates, wars and alliances on stelae; the rivalry between Tikal and Calakmul dominated the 6th and 7th centuries. Between 800 and 950 most cities of the southern lowlands were depopulated, in a collapse whose causes—droughts, war, overpopulation—are debated.

regiones/area-maya/eras.3.resumen.texto: The center shifts to northern Yucatán, with Chichén Itzá and then Mayapán (around 1220–1450); in the Guatemalan highlands the K'iche' and Kaqchikel kingdoms form. When the Spanish arrive, Yucatán is divided into many rival provinces.

regiones/area-maya/eras.4.resumen.texto: Pedro de Alvarado conquers the Guatemalan highlands from 1524, with Nahua and Kaqchikel allies, and the Montejo family conquers Yucatán between 1527 and 1546, with the founding of Mérida in 1542. The Itzá of Tayasal, in Petén, resisted until 1697.

regiones/area-maya/eras.5.resumen.texto: Encomiendas, repartimientos and Indian towns under the Audiencia of Guatemala and the governorship of Yucatán; the Tzeltal (1712) and Jacinto Canek (1761) rebellions were suppressed.

regiones/area-maya/eras.6.resumen.texto: The region is divided between Mexico, Guatemala and the British settlement of Belize. In 1847 the Maya of eastern Yucatán rose up in the Caste War, which lasted until the capture of Chan Santa Cruz in 1901.

regiones/area-maya/eras.7.resumen.texto: In the Guatemalan civil war (1960–1996) some 200,000 people were killed or disappeared; the Commission for Historical Clarification attributed the great majority of violations to the state and classified the massacres of Maya people in 1981–1983 as acts of genocide. In 1994 the Zapatista Army rose up in Chiapas.

regiones/area-maya/demografia.0.nota.texto: Extrapolation from the lidar survey of northern Guatemala to the central lowlands (about 95,000 km²) in the Late Classic (650–800); it does not include the highlands or northern Yucatán. Archaeological population estimates are very uncertain.

regiones/area-maya/religiones.1.nombre.texto: Maya religion (gods of maize and rain, ancestor veneration, sacred kingship, self-sacrifice and human sacrifice)

regiones/area-maya/religiones.3.nombre.texto: Catholicism (with confraternities, patron saints and Maya practices)

regiones/area-maya/religiones.4.nombre.texto: Traditional Maya religion (keepers of the 260-day calendar) and syncretic cults such as the Talking Cross

regiones/area-maya/religiones.5.nombre.texto: Protestant and evangelical churches (Presbyterian mission in Guatemala since 1882)

regiones/area-maya/religiones.1.nota.texto: The stelae and murals of Bonampak show the capture and sacrifice of prisoners; in the sacred cenote of Chichén Itzá, the remains of more than a hundred people, many of them children, were found.

regiones/area-maya/religiones.4.nota.texto: In 1562 Friar Diego de Landa led a trial against idolatry at Maní in which thousands of Maya were tortured and codices and images were burned.

regiones/area-maya/culturas.2.nombre.texto: Maya (Yucatec, Chontal, Chol, Tzeltal, Tzotzil, K'iche's, Kaqchikel, Q'eqchi's, Mam and others)

regiones/area-maya/culturas.2.nota.texto: In western Chiapas lived the Zoque, speakers of a Mixe-Zoquean language; in southeastern Guatemala, the Xinca, and from the Postclassic, Pipil speakers of Nahuatl on the Pacific coast of Guatemala and western El Salvador.

regiones/area-maya/culturas.4.nota.texto: At the end of the 18th century Indians were still about two-thirds or more of the population of Guatemala and Yucatán.

regiones/area-maya/culturas.5.nota.texto: The shift to a non-Indigenous majority depends on how it is counted: in Guatemala's 2018 census 42% identified as Maya, and in Yucatán more than half the population identifies as Indigenous, although fewer than a third speak Maya.

regiones/area-maya/idiomas.1.nombre.texto: Mayan languages (Yucatec, Chontal, Chol, Tzeltal, Tzotzil, K'iche', Kaqchikel, Q'eqchi', Mam and others)

regiones/area-maya/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Classic inscriptions record mainly a prestige language related to Chol, the “Classic Cholan” (Houston, Robertson and Stuart, 2000).

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/resumen.texto: The Amazon basin in Brazil, from the borders with Peru, Colombia and Venezuela to the mouth near Belém, including Amapá, Acre, Rondônia and northern Mato Grosso. Archaeology has found sedentary, hierarchical societies—Marajoara, Santarém, the villages of the upper Xingu—that transformed the soil (terra preta) and the forest; how many people lived there before the conquest is debated. From 1616 the Portuguese advanced from Belém with missions and expeditions to capture Indigenous people, and rubber (1879–1912), roads and 20th-century deforestation transformed the region.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.0.resum.texto: In the Pedra Pintada Cave, in Monte Alegre, there are paintings and remains of hunter-gatherers about 13,000 years old (Roosevelt et al., 1996).

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.1.resum.texto: In the shell middens of Taperinha, near Santarém, there is pottery about 7,000 years old, among the oldest in the Americas, and manioc was already cultivated in the southwestern Amazon.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.2.resum.texto: On Marajó Island, the Marajoara culture (around 400–1400) built mounds and produced polychrome pottery; in Santarém the Tapajó flourished, and in the upper Xingu, villages linked by roads and ditches (around 1250–1650). The geoglyphs of Acre and the dark earths (terra preta) show a forest modified by people.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.3.resum.texto: Francisco de Orellana sailed down the river in 1542; his chronicler, Gaspar de Carvajal, described densely populated banks and battles with female warriors, from which the river's name comes. Ursúa and Lope de Aguirre followed (1560–1561).

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.4.resum.texto: The Portuguese founded Belém in 1616, and Pedro Teixeira went up the river to Quito (1637–1639). The “rescue troops” captured Indigenous people to enslave them, while Jesuits such as Antônio Vieira, Franciscans and Carmelites gathered them into missions.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.5.resum.texto: Pombal took the government of the villages away from the religious orders and created the Directorate (1757), which imposed Portuguese. In the Cabanagem (1835–1840), a rebellion of mestizos, Indigenous people and poor Black people in Pará, between 30,000 and 40,000 people died according to estimates.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.6.resum.texto: Global demand for rubber attracts hundreds of thousands of migrants from the northeast and enriches Manaus and Belém; rubber gatherers subjected people to forced labor and killed many Indigenous people. Brazil buys Acre from Bolivia in 1903.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.7.resum.texto: Asian rubber sinks the Amazonian economy; the Indian Protection Service (1910), led by Cândido Rondon, seeks to contact and protect the peoples of the interior, and Fordlândia (1928) fails as a plantation.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/eras.8.resum.texto: The military dictatorship opens the Transamazonian Highway (from 1970) and encourages colonization; deforestation and illegal mining advance into the forest. The 1988 Constitution recognizes Indigenous lands, such as the Yanomami land (1992).

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/religiones.0.texto: Amazonian religions (shamanism, initiation rites, sacred flutes)

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/religiones.2.texto: Catholicism (Jesuit, Franciscan and Carmelite missions and, from 1757, Directorate villages)

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/religiones.6.texto: Pentecostalism (the Assembly of God was born in Belém in 1911) and other evangelical churches

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/religiones.2.texto: Outside the villages, most of the peoples of the interior were not baptized.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/culturas.1.n.texto: Amazonian peoples (Marajoara, Tapajó, Arawak, Tupi, Carib, Ye, Pano, Tukano and many others)

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/culturas.4.n.texto: Brazilians (caboclos, riverine people and migrants from other regions)

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/culturas.1.n.texto: Denevan (1992) estimated about 5.7 million inhabitants for the whole Greater Amazonia around 1492; other authors give much lower or higher figures.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/culturas.4.n.texto: Approximate date: non-Indigenous people become the majority with the rubber boom.

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/idiomas.1.no.texto: Amazonian languages: Arawakan, Tupian, Cariban, Macro-Jê, Pano, Tucanoan and many others

regiones/amazonia-brasilena/idiomas.3.no.texto: It was the common language of colonial society in Pará and on the Rio Negro; in the interior, hundreds of Indigenous languages were still spoken.
